title: NovaEdge — Dedicated capacity discovery
summary: Discovery call to scope Dedicated GPU capacity for NovaEdge analytics workloads. Discussed traffic profile, isolation/VPC needs, burst strategy (burst to hosted vs reserved buffer), scaling targets, compliance requirements (SOC2/KMS), and next steps: pricing, security pack, and benchmark run.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-13
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Lina (CTO), Aaron (Head of ML), Sophie (Infra)

Summary: quick discovery to scope Dedicated reserved GPUs; customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency-sensitive analytics workloads.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this one, with Carlos our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Lina: Good, thanks. Busy month but excited to chat.
[00:12] Carlos: Quick agenda — hear your workloads, traffic, security needs, talk about Dedicated options and burst/fallback strategies, then next steps, cool?
[00:20] Aaron: Yep, sounds good. I'll start with context — NovaEdge runs a real-time analytics layer on top of a set of transformers for entity extraction, reranking, and short-form summarization. Right now it's on managed infra (k8s with GPU nodes on-cloud) but costs are creeping up and tail latency during batch windows is spiking.
[00:40] Sophie: We also have regulatory constraints for EU customers, and we need audit logs and customer data isolation, so multi-tenant hosted is tricky for some customers.
[00:52] Maya: Totally makes sense. When you say tail latency spikes — what's the p95/p99 and token sizes roughly?
[00:58] Aaron: p95 is around 450ms for our main pipeline, p99 is 1.8s during nightly batch windows. Typical requests are ~450 tokens (input+output) but we do a lot of short requests too, like 50-120 tokens for certain endpoints.
[01:18] Carlos: Helpful — that distribution matters because batching behavior changes with seq lengths. Do you have QPS numbers or peak concurrent requests?
[01:26] Aaron: Normal load is ~40-60 qps, peaks up to 400 qps for 10-15 minutes during some storefront events. We expect those peaks to grow 2x next year.
[01:38] Maya: Ok so predictable baseline with short but sharp bursts — that's exactly the type where Dedicated with burst capacity can help. How are you thinking about commitment vs burst?
[01:48] Lina: We're open to a committed baseline to control costs, but need to handle those spikes without 10x provisioning. Ideally burst to additional reserved or shared capacity.
[01:58] Carlos: Two common patterns: 1) Reserve baseline Dedicated GPU pool sized for steady-state and autoscale with a buffer for short bursts — autoscale can add nodes in ~2-5 minutes depending on provisioning model; 2) Have baseline Dedicated + allow overflow to Redwood Hosted endpoints for very short spikes where strict isolation isn't required. The second requires policy decisions around data residency and compliance.
[02:22] Sophie: Overflow to Hosted is a non-starter for EU-regulated customers, at least for those datasets. We could use overflow only for anonymized or non-regulated traffic.
[02:34] Maya: Makes sense — Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) is also an option if you need fully isolated control plane. For Dedicated we can also offer regional isolation and KMS integration so keys never leave your account.
[02:48] Aaron: On that KMS topic — do you have HSM support or only cloud KMS? We have strict key management policies.
[02:56] Carlos: We integrate with customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK) and HSM partners for Private deployments. For Dedicated in our managed region we support CMEK — HSM may be available as part of Private/on-prem. I'll share the exact matrix after the call, apologies if the doc calls it "Redwood Dedicate" sometimes in our notes.
[03:18] Lina: No worries. For sizing, we were thinking initial pilot could be 4x A100-ish equivalents for a two-week benchmark, then scale up to ~16 GPUs for production peaks. Is that a normal path?
[03:30] Carlos: Absolutely. Pilot with 4 GPUs to validate latency and cost per token, then grow. We recommend running a benchmark with your actual payloads and batching profile; that helps pick kernel/quantization configs.
[03:42] Aaron: On autoscaling, how quickly can you spin up additional GPUs? If peaks are only 10-15 minutes, waiting 5 minutes to provision might still be problematic.
[03:52] Maya: There are a couple levers — warm spare buffer (keep a small extra pool hot), pre-warmed nodes, and hybrid overflow to Hosted. If provisioning latency is a blocker, a warm spare or short pre-warm policy is common. You pay a little more for the hot buffer but avoid p99 spikes.
[04:14] Sophie: What's the pricing model for keeping a warm spare? Is that part of committed capacity or a separate charge?
[04:20] Maya: Typically it's part of Dedicated capacity — you can size committed pool to include buffer. We also offer burst credits or hourly burst on top of committed for short-term events. I'll send a few example pricing tiers.
[04:32] Aaron: Good. On observability — we need token-level latency, model per-route cost breakdown, and tracing hooks to tie traces back to downstream services.
[04:42] Carlos: Redwood Console exposes per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, and we have tracing integrations (OpenTelemetry). There are export hooks for logs and audit trails for compliance.
[04:55] Lina: About network — we need a VPC peering/privatelink approach; can Dedicated live in our VPC?
[05:03] Carlos: Dedicated runs in Redwood-managed infra but we support VPC peering or PrivateLink and customer-managed VPC options for Private deployments. For Dedicated we can set up VPC Peering and private endpoints with strict ingress controls. We have a network checklist (we'll share) and typical firewall rules.
[05:20] Sophie: Any special requirements for latency-sensitive routing? We need sub-100ms inter-service within EU region.
[05:27] Carlos: If all services are in the same region and you use private networking, sub-100ms inter-service is achievable; we'll run node-level RT tests during the pilot. There may be differences by provider and instance type.
[05:40] Aaron: One more — model variants and fallbacks. We want graceful degradation if the big LLM isn't available: fall back to smaller quantized models. Can Redwood route automatically?
[05:50] Maya: Yes — smart routing policies let you prefer a primary variant and automatically fallback to a compatible quantized variant or a cheaper model when capacity's constrained. That can be per-route.
[05:59] Lina: Great. On compliance, we need SOC2 Type II, ISO27001? Also SSO — SAML and RBAC for console access.
[06:08] Carlos: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO docs; SAML SSO and RBAC are available for Dedicated and Private consoles. We'll attach the security pack.
[06:18] Aaron: Timeline: we'd like pilot in Jan, production in Q1 if benchmarks look good. Budget owner is infra and procurement — likely a 12-month committed capacity.
[06:28] Maya: Sounds reasonable. For the pilot we'll do a 2-week benchmark with 4 GPUs, run your traffic profile, measure p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens. Then we can model committed tiers for 12 months.
[06:40] Sophie: For the benchmark, we can provide a replay of production traffic and sample payloads — any particular format?
[06:46] Carlos: JSON lines with timestamp, request payload, and model settings is ideal. We'll also need your tokenization settings to replicate batching.
[06:54] Lina: Ok we'll prepare that.
[06:56] Maya: To recap action items — we'll send pricing and security docs, Carlos will share network checklist and Dedicated architecture doc, and we'll propose benchmark dates. Follow up meeting Dec 20 to align on pricing and legal contacts.
[07:10] Aaron: Thanks all.
[07:12] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.
